paras: The Washington Circle pursuit of Coleman Saunders was a crowd chase of a Black man through the streets of Washington, D.C., on the night of August 3, 1910, after he was accused of striking a park watchman, Presley Griffin. According to The Washington Herald, nearly 100 men and boys joined the hunt with cries of "Lynch him!" and broke into the shanty where he hid, but he escaped through a rear window. Police arrested Saunders the next afternoon, and he was later indicted for assault with a dangerous weapon.

Saunders, a 25-year-old man described as "colored" and "a mulatto," had been sleeping on benches in Washington Circle and had been told several times to keep out of the park. The Washington Times reported a police explanation that a metropolitan policeman had awakened him that night by striking the soles of his shoes with a club, and that Saunders believed Griffin had done it.

Shortly before or about 11:30 p.m., Griffin, a 37-year-old park watchman from Old Dominion Heights, Virginia, again ordered Saunders off a bench and was struck behind the right ear. The papers named the weapon differently: a blackjack in the Herald's headline, a stone in the Evening Star, and a brick in the Times and in the later court reports.

As Griffin fell unconscious, Saunders ran, and according to the Herald, cries of "Lynch him!" and "Catch the man!" went up as several men gave chase and pedestrians joined in. The Herald named S. L. Daw, John Linnon, J. W. Quigley and Volney Eaton as leading the crowd along Twenty-second street to the corner of L street, where Saunders entered the shanty of his sister, Mary Sanders. The crowd burst through the locked door and searched the house from cellar to roof, only to learn that he had escaped through a rear window into an alley.

Meanwhile Lieut. James Hartley called out every detective and policeman in the city to look for him. About 2:30 p.m. on August 4, Capt. Daley of the ninth precinct, with Sergt. Whelan and Policemen Sutton and Anderson, found Saunders hiding under a bed in a house on 14th street northeast.

Saunders was held on a charge of assault with a dangerous weapon, and the Evening Star noted that policemen from two precincts subjected him to a "sweating" after his arrest. Unable to furnish bond, he was sent to jail on August 5 while the hearing waited on Griffin's condition, which the papers described variously as recovering or dangerous. On August 9 he admitted the blow in Police Court and was committed by Judge Aukam for the grand jury on a $2,000 bond, reportedly having told police he was drunk and "mad and frightened" when he struck.
The grand jury indicted him for assault with a dangerous weapon on September 29. No report of a trial, or of any action against members of the crowd, appears in the coverage.

Three Washington dailies covered the case, all as a story of an assault on a park officer by a "negro." Only the Herald made the crowd part of its headline, with "Crowd of Hundred Join in Hunt for Assailant," and it reported the lynch cries and the break-in without comment. The Evening Star headlined "Threw Stone in Revenge," said Saunders had "murderously assaulted" the watchman, and mentioned only that several persons pursued him.
Follow-up items in the Herald and the Star tracked the arrest, the Police Court hearings and the indictment, without returning to the crowd. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

The size and intent of the crowd rest on the Herald alone, which counted nearly 100 men and boys crying "Lynch him!", while the Evening Star described a pursuit by several people in the park and placed the escape at a relative's house on 26th street.

reader.title: Washington Circle pursuit of Coleman Saunders
bases: The Herald reported a crowd of nearly 100 hunting a Black man with cries of 'Lynch him!' and breaking into the house where he hid, an attempted lynching that ended when he escaped and was later arrested by police (A1, A2, A6).

No one was killed: Saunders escaped the pursuers and was arrested by police the next afternoon (A2, A4, A6). The Herald's account of a crowd of about 100 crying 'Lynch him!' after an alleged assault describes an attempt, not a completed lynching (A1, A2).

The Herald and the Evening Star independently report the assault, a pursuit by people in the park and Saunders's escape through a relative's house (A2, A3, A4); the crowd of about 100 and the lynch cries appear only in the Herald (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Washington Herald
accounts.gist: Saunders knocked Griffin unconscious; nearly 100 men and boys joined a manhunt with cries of 'Lynch him!', burst into his sister's shanty and searched it, but he had fled through a rear window.

accounts.label: Evening Star
accounts.gist: Saunders threw a stone at Griffin in revenge for being driven from the park; several people in the park pursued him, but he escaped through a relative's house on 26th street; nothing about lynch cries.

accounts.label: Police theory (Washington Times)
accounts.gist: Some police said a metropolitan policeman had struck the soles of Saunders's shoes with his club to wake him, and Saunders believed Griffin had done it; Griffin said he was struck with a brick.

accounts.label: Saunders's alleged confession
accounts.gist: Saunders was quoted as saying he was intoxicated, was woken by the policeman, and struck him while 'mad and frightened'.

framing.detail: The Herald headlined 'PARK WATCHMAN BEATEN BY NEGRO' and 'Crowd of Hundred Join in Hunt for Assailant', reporting the lynch cries and the break-in without comment and naming the crowd's leaders.
The Evening Star headlined 'ASSAULT ON WATCHMAN' and 'Threw Stone in Revenge', said Saunders 'murderously assaulted' the watchman, and reported the post-arrest 'sweating' matter-of-factly.
The Washington Times headlined 'Negro Who Slugged Presley Griffin May Have Sought Revenge' and gave a police explanation for the attack.

record_check.dossier: Coleman Saunders (Sanders) alone was the crowd's target; Presley Griffin was the injured park watchman and complainant, not a victim of the crowd.
Saunders is described as 'colored', 'negro' and 'a mulatto': Black.

record_check.record: accused of assaulting a park watchman
record_check.dossier: Accused of striking Park Watchman Presley Griffin on the head (blackjack, stone or brick) after being ordered off a bench in Washington Circle.
Griffin was a park watchman ('Waterman' is an OCR error); the assault is an accusation, later admitted in Police Court.

record_check.record: he had escaped through a rear window
record_check.dossier: Correct, but the record omits his arrest by police the next afternoon, the Police Court committal and the September indictment.
Pursuit, threat (lynch cries) and breaking into a house; the 'beating' was the blow to Griffin, not violence against Saunders.
The Herald names S. L. Daw, John Linnon, J. W. Quigley and Volney Eaton as leading the crowd.
No injury to Saunders by the crowd is reported (his arm was already bound from an earlier brick blow, per the Herald).
Three Washington white dailies (Herald, Evening Star, Times), 11 articles from August 4 to September 30; no Black-press coverage found.

info: Wednesday night, August 3, 1910, about 11 to 11:30 p.m., with the hunt lasting into the early morning of August 4
Washington Circle, Washington, D.C.; pursuit along Twenty-second street to a house near L street (Herald) or on 26th street (Star)
Coleman Saunders (Sanders in the Herald's first story), 25, described as 'colored', 'negro' and 'a mulatto', target of the pursuit
Accused of striking Park Watchman (park policeman) Presley Griffin on the head after being ordered off a bench; weapon given as a blackjack, a blunt instrument, a stone or a brick
Pedestrians and people in the park; the Herald names S. L. Daw, John Linnon, J. W. Quigley and Volney Eaton as leading the crowd
Saunders escaped the crowd, was arrested by police, admitted the blow in Police Court and was indicted; no report of a trial was found
